voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
The Son of God, fully what the Father is - not a likeness, not a lesser copy. In our years the palace pressed a softer word on us: the Son is *like* the Father, they said, a careful likeness. Bishops we loved lost their churches and went into exile rather than sign it. From Nicaea we inherited one word and carried it like a banner: *homoousios* - of the same being. It is not a word found in Scripture. We fought over it because it was the most exact word we had for what needed saying.

But ask what he was *to us*, and the deepest answer is what he does. Our teachers said salvation itself is becoming god by grace - *theōsis*, our boldest word. The creature grows into God's own likeness, and the gap between creature and Maker never closes. That is why the fight mattered: if the Son makes gods of us, the Son cannot be a creature, because no creature makes gods.

And we met him where our whole life started - at the water. We were baptized into his Name with the Father and the Spirit, and the words said over us were treated as our charter: believe as you were baptized, because the formula spoken over you already carries the whole confession.

glosses.plain_meaning: We taught that salvation means becoming god by grace. A person grows endlessly into likeness with a God no mind can measure. Becoming god by grace never meant becoming equal to God. The creature never crosses the gap that separates it from its maker.
glosses.quick_meaning: Deification, or becoming god by grace. Our boldest word for what salvation finally is.

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
He became human so that we might become god by grace. That is the heart of it - not a legal transaction first, but God entering our sickness to heal it from inside. We spoke of his death as a ransom paid, a debt settled. One of our teachers put it this way: "That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange... so that humanity, by its communion with the divine, might itself be made divine".

He also taught us where to find him after he rose. The hungry, the naked, the stranger at the door - mercy to them is meeting Christ. Our preachers took that teaching at full strength: the poor bear the very image of God, so whatever you keep beyond your own need already belongs to them. In a famine year that conviction opened barns and fed villages. Later it became buildings - a guest-house, an infirmary, a house where lepers were washed and fed by people who chose that work.

So what he did: he crossed the gap we could not cross, made us sharers in God's own life, and left himself standing at every door where the destitute wait.

sources.spoken_rendering: That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
Becoming god by grace - not equal to God, but truly made like him, endlessly. The gap between creature and Creator never closes. We are not turned into what God is by nature; we grow into his likeness by what he freely gives.

One of our teachers put it plainly: "God was born among men... so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine - rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice". The physician enters the sickness to heal it from inside. Christ crosses the gap we could not cross, and by communion with him we are made sharers in what he is.

One teacher among us - Gregory of Nyssa - argued that because God has no limit, the soul's growth toward him has no finish line either. Arriving completely would mean love itself running out, so the reaching never stops. That teaching is his own development, not the whole circle's shared property, and we say so honestly.

So *theōsis* means this: salvation as a real transformation, not a legal verdict alone - the creature remade in God's image, growing endlessly into his likeness, by grace, without ever becoming God by nature.

references.spoken_rendering: That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: cappadocian
voice_event.text:
We believed it because we were baptized into it before we could weigh it. The formula was said over us - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and we were taught to believe as we had been baptized, because those words already carried the whole confession. Reception came before analysis. The faith was not something we concluded; it was something we were signed into, and our whole life afterward was the slow understanding of what had already been given.

But the fight that sharpened it came from worship itself. Basil, at the evening lamps, gave glory to the Father together with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit - not merely through the Son in the Spirit, the older form. Some objected: too much was being claimed. His answer became a book, and in it he argued that baptism, belief, and the giving of glory stand or fall together as one sequence. He wrote: "The Lord handed down to us, as essential and saving teaching, that the Holy Spirit is to be ranked together with the Father".

So we believed it because the water said it first, and we defended it because worship itself was at stake - the very words we sang carried the faith we fought for.
